entry.title: How Lola Madrid turns crazy ambition into serious work
entry.summary: Creative Insight How Lola Madrid turns crazy ambition into serious work The Spanish agency has released a steady stream of striking work this year for the likes of De’Longhi and Magnum, proving that their mantra is working By Adam Woodward 18/11/2026 3:44 am Under executive creat
entry.content:
Creative Insight

How Lola Madrid turns crazy ambition into serious work

The Spanish agency has released a steady stream of striking work this year for the likes of De’Longhi and Magnum, proving that their mantra is working

By Adam Woodward 18/11/2026 3:44 am

Under executive creative director Tomás Ostiglia, Lola Madrid has built a reputation for producing work that can look slick one minute and strange, even slightly unruly, the next – but always rooted in a clear point of view.

Lola’s approach has been distilled into a recently unveiled positioning: ‘Crazy ambition makes serious things happen.’ This sounds like a contradiction: how can you be ‘crazy’ and ‘serious’ at the same time? “I think most of the time, you’re not always 100% sure about what you’re doing,” Ostiglia elaborates. “We’re crazy ambitious, but we have the conviction to make really serious things happen. You follow the idea. That’s how we work.”

That thinking is increasingly evident in Lola’s work for brands including Magnum, Axe/Lynx and De’Longhi, while the agency itself now reaches far beyond its home in the Spanish capital. Originally conceived within the MullenLowe network by Fernando Vega Olmos in 2007 as a boutique, pan-European agency, with Unilever as its founding client, Lola has since become a global operation with hubs in New York, Los Angeles and São Paulo, all sitting within TBWA Worldwide. Yet Madrid remains its gravitational centre.

entry.title: Wunder Werkz gives Denver Design District a new identity
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Wunder Werkz gives Denver Design District a new identity The design studio has created a bold visual identity for the area as it expands beyond interior design professionals and fosters a retail, food and arts hub By Rebecca Fulleylove 18/11/2026 3:40 am Wund
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Wunder Werkz gives Denver Design District a new identity

The design studio has created a bold visual identity for the area as it expands beyond interior design professionals and fosters a retail, food and arts hub

By Rebecca Fulleylove 18/11/2026 3:40 am

Wunder Werkz has developed a new identity for Denver Design District, as the Colorado neighbourhood looks to broaden its appeal beyond the interior design trade.

Once primarily a destination for industry professionals, the area is now looking to attract a wider audience through a growing mix of design retail, art, food and other cultural offerings.

“The idea was to make a more welcoming, accessible district; one that celebrates design in all its forms,” explains Jon Hartman, partner at Wunder Werkz.

“Trade remains an important part of the ecosystem, but it is no longer the whole story. So, we needed to design a brand that felt open and culturally relevant while still carrying the credibility of the design industry.”

The identity starts with a palette of brick, blush, slate and deep yellow, bringing brighter tones to an area otherwise characterised by the tans and greys of its built environment. Its central mark, formed from three progressively compressed Ds, takes a geometric approach. Designed to feel both solid and in motion, it provides a shorthand for the district’s name.

Wunder Werkz has also developed DDD Standard, a bespoke mid-weight sans serif used across the wordmark and wider identity. Loosely referencing the mid-century furniture forms of Herbert Bayer, the typeface balances architectural structure with more playful details.

Its numerals were given particular attention, with large-scale applications such as building identification and signage in mind. A set of silhouetted product icons completes the graphics, depicting different design categories and helping visitors find their way around.

Beyond just printed materials and digital branding, the identity has been carried onto the buildings themselves. Each has been given its own colour designation, repeated across external signage, directories and other navigational elements.

The approach is also visible in a new sculptural aluminium sign for Denver Design District, installed alongside Herbert Bayer’s Articulated Wall, which has stood in the area since the 1980s.

The website has undergone a similar rethink. Bringing together shop directories, maps, events and editorial content, it caters to both regular trade visitors looking for specific businesses and newcomers wanting to get a better sense of what the district has to offer.

entry.title: Jonathan Glazer directs uncanny short film for Gentle Monster
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Jonathan Glazer directs uncanny short film for Gentle Monster The cinematic ad campaign stars Joaquin Phoenix and offers a first look at Gentle Monster’s intelligent eyewear collection By Eliza Williams 17/11/2026 2:03 pm Reality and fantasy blur in Jonathan
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Jonathan Glazer directs uncanny short film for Gentle Monster

The cinematic ad campaign stars Joaquin Phoenix and offers a first look at Gentle Monster’s intelligent eyewear collection

By Eliza Williams 17/11/2026 2:03 pm

Reality and fantasy blur in Jonathan Glazer’s compelling new short film, which sees Joaquin Phoenix play a salesman who has a series of strange encounters in an impeccably designed hotel, which become increasingly dreamlike and bizarre.

Echoing both Stanley Kubrick’s classic film The Shining and recent A24 hit Backrooms, the film’s weird moments begin early on, when Phoenix experiences a deeply odd interaction at the check-in desk. He nonetheless takes this in his stride, and soon settles into his mid-century modern suite.

Yet when he is awoken from a nap by mysterious noises, he is compelled to investigate. The film then takes a turn for the surreal as time bends and Phoenix alights upon a pair of unexpected characters in the midst of a fight.

Phoenix once again shows remarkable composure in the face of the bizarre, and instead of immediately getting the hell out of there, he turns to his Gentle Monster glasses for assistance, using their in-built tech to translate and communicate with the creatures and make sense of the new world he has discovered.

The film certainly stands apart from the intelligent eyewear advertising we’ve been presented with from other brands, proving to be a product demo of the most surreal kind while retaining the deep fashion associations we have with Gentle Monster. Plus Glazer’s direction is witty, odd and beautiful, and – as ever – impossible to look away from.

entry.title: Pentagram rebrands Greece’s Alpha Bank around legacy symbol
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Pentagram rebrands Greece’s Alpha Bank around legacy symbol Based on an ancient Greek coin, the bank’s primary symbol forms the centrepiece of a striking new identity that blends heritage with contemporary design By Daniel Milroy Maher 17/11/2026 3:25 am Alph
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Pentagram rebrands Greece’s Alpha Bank around legacy symbol

Based on an ancient Greek coin, the bank’s primary symbol forms the centrepiece of a striking new identity that blends heritage with contemporary design

By Daniel Milroy Maher 17/11/2026 3:25 am

Alpha Bank, one of Greece’s oldest and largest financial groups, has partnered with Pentagram on a new identity, inspired by its rich history. Established in 1879, the Athens-based bank has been a central figure in Greek society ever since its founding, sponsoring and preserving Greek culture and heritage for decades.

Now, amid a shifting financial landscape, and with desires to modernise the business, Alpha Bank felt it was time to refresh and future-proof its branding. The brief for the Pentagram team was to develop an identity that could maintain Alpha Bank’s competitive position within the market, while appealing to a broad demographic of young professionals and affluent older customers, as well as societal and institutional stakeholders.

Pentagram partner Domenic Lippa, who led the project, says that Alpha Bank was an ideal collaborator from the outset, and “was willing to explore different opportunities, and in doing so, push the brief further”. He continues: “Once that creative door was opened, we could go in different directions, but what I felt quite early was that the emotional strength of the legacy was the symbol.”

The symbol Lippa refers to is, of course, the Alpha Bank logo, which has remained the same since its founding nearly 150 years ago. It is based on an ancient Greek coin called a silver stater, one of which can be found in the Bank’s extensive numismatic collection. Emerging in the 8th century BC, the stater was the first coin to be used in the markets of the Mediterranean and the East, and served as an ideal muse for one of the country’s premier banks.

However, feeling that Alpha Bank’s stater symbol “had lost some of its quality” over time, Lippa and his team chose to gently rework the logo, separating the graphic element from the wordmark and redrawing it so that it appears thinner, elongated and more contemporary. Lippa explains: “The symbol needed to become the emotional heart for the brand. Like it was originally. For this to happen, we needed to liberate it from the wordmark. The wordmark itself needed to be less formal but still retain the authority for the bank.”

Where the wordmark is concerned, Pentagram chose to replace the old font with new custom typefaces, called Alpha Sans and Alpha Text. The former, developed in partnership with type designer Tom Baber, features five different weights and does much of the heavy lifting across the identity, while the latter serves as a functional typeface for use at smaller sizes.

Colour was also an important consideration for the design team, and offered yet another chance to champion Alpha Bank’s strong heritage. Revolving around the existing Alpha Blue, which has been at the heart of the bank’s identity for decades, Pentagram added new key colours such as white and Galazio Blue, as well as a secondary palette of Thalassi Turquoise, Heritage Pink and Alpha Gold. Five other brighter hues were also introduced to be used for digital elements such as infographics.

Along with the logo and colour palette, Pentagram developed a series of abstract and logo patterns inspired by aspects of the Alpha Bank symbol; a series of useful brand icons also based on the symbol; and a suite of striking brand imagery that captures real people and everyday moments to evoke feelings of trust and positivity.

Together, these elements make for an identity that is deeply rooted in Alpha Bank’s past, and at the same time heavily invested in its future. Cleaner, sharper and better equipped for the digital age, it also retains the bank’s reputation for warmth and dependability.

Reflecting on the project’s success, Lippa notes: “I believe within any project we are eternally searching for the truth in the solution. To discover the truth, you need a client willing to help you go on that journey. The team at Alpha Bank gave us 110% of their time, knowledge and ambition. Without them we would never have managed to find what we were searching for.”

entry.summary: Creative Leadership A look inside a great CMO-agency relationship When a brand CMO and its ad agency are attuned strategically and creatively, magic – and money – can follow. Here, we examine the results of the recent partnership between Telstra and agency Bear Meets Eagle On Fir
entry.content:
Creative Leadership

A look inside a great CMO-agency relationship

When a brand CMO and its ad agency are attuned strategically and creatively, magic – and money – can follow. Here, we examine the results of the recent partnership between Telstra and agency Bear Meets Eagle On Fire

By Eliza Williams 17/11/2026 3:10 am

In March this year, it was announced that Brent Smart, CMO at Australian telco Telstra since 2022, was stepping down. On the surface, this might seem like no big deal. After all, CMOs move on from brands with increasing haste these days. But Smart had brought huge change to Telstra and, in partnership with Micah Walker and the team at Sydney-based agency Bear Meets Eagle On Fire, is credited with reinvigorating the brand.

Reflecting on the Telstra he joined in 2022, Smart acknowledges that while the “business was in great shape”, the brand reputation wasn’t. “Telstra was a brand people didn’t like much,” he says. “Most of the budget was going into retail offers and performance marketing – any brand work was very corporate. They created a huge volume of work but it was pretty templated and forgettable. I had a clear narrative from the get-go that would guide all our work and link it back to the reputation challenge – if you want to change how people feel about the brand, you need to change how the brand feels.”

Smart and Walker had worked together before on projects for insurance company IAG, where Bear created work for the firm’s largest brand, NRMA, and also created a new digital insurance brand, Rollin’, from scratch. “When I joined Telstra, I wanted the same sort of thinking and level of craft that Bear always brings,” says Smart. “I see Micah as more of a partner than an agency creative leader. I welcome his push – there’s no one’s taste I trust more.”

entry.title: New book charts Tadanori Yokoo’s illustrious career
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration New book charts Tadanori Yokoo’s illustrious career Edited by Mark Holborn, this detailed retrospective delves into the striking work and living legacy of the famed Japanese visual artist By Daniel Milroy Maher 16/11/2026 10:07 am Thames & Hudson has released
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

New book charts Tadanori Yokoo’s illustrious career

Edited by Mark Holborn, this detailed retrospective delves into the striking work and living legacy of the famed Japanese visual artist

By Daniel Milroy Maher 16/11/2026 10:07 am

Thames & Hudson has released the first comprehensive English-language retrospective of famed Japanese visual artist Tadanori Yokoo. The new publication spans Yokoo’s entire career, from his emergence in the 1960s in Tokyo to his ongoing work at the age of 90.

Born in Nishikawa in 1936, Yokoo’s first foray into the creative industry was as a commercial designer, which, while restrictive, gave him the technical foundation he needed to refine, and later to expand, his personal practice.

He soon moved to Tokyo, where his work drifted into the avant-garde, and his experimental approach to graphic design, illustration and painting earned him a reputation (especially among the city’s radical youth) as a groundbreaking visual artist. Over the years, this reputation grew, solidifying his place as one of Japan’s most celebrated cultural figures.

In this monograph, readers can explore his unique blend of original pre-psychedelic imagery, Pop Art, sexual iconography, and references to Japanese historical tradition, such as ukiyo-e prints. Presented chronologically, the featured work also traces Yokoo’s evolving focal points throughout his life, from post-war consumer culture in the 60s to spirituality and mysticism in the 70s, and then finally to memory and mortality from the 80s onwards.

The latter theme is particularly prominent in Yokoo’s story, with Holborn writing in the book’s introduction that “the beginning [of his story], in fact, lies not in the early graphic work, although that provides a visual introduction, but in memory…. As he gets older, his memory becomes increasingly pertinent. The resource of the subconscious, from which the work arises, becomes yet more pronounced, and so the events of the past determine what comes from Yokoo’s brush in his studio [today].”

Across the chapters of the book, readers are given similar insights into the interests, beliefs and sensibilities of Yokoo. There are many quotes from previous interviews he has given, in which he discusses his creative process, the themes of his work, and his world view more generally. His influence on, and collaborations with, other writers and artists are also explored – most notably his work with the renowned Japanese novelist and playwright Yukio Mishima.

Crucially, for Holborn, editing this book was about more than just documenting Yokoo’s fascinating and extensive oeuvre; it was also a long-term effort to “reinforce the narrative of his life”. As the author explains, “His work defines that narrative. Here, I am simply joining up the threads as they become evident in the course of the work.”

Tadanori Yokoo is published by Thames & Hudson; thamesandhudsonusa.com

entry.title: The Conversation: The state of freelancing
entry.summary: Creative Insight The Conversation: The state of freelancing With more creatives pushed towards flexible work, and agencies rethinking how they hire and deploy talent, the industry is facing a critical question: can this new model work for everyone? By Adam Woodward 16/11/2026 3:2
entry.content:
Creative Insight

The Conversation: The state of freelancing

With more creatives pushed towards flexible work, and agencies rethinking how they hire and deploy talent, the industry is facing a critical question: can this new model work for everyone?

By Adam Woodward 16/11/2026 3:25 am

For much of the creative industries, freelancing has long been a fact of life. According to a report published by the UK government in September, last year 28.5% of the creative industries’ workforce were self-employed – almost twice the rate of the wider economy. Yet the freelance model is being reshaped by tighter budgets, agency restructures, fewer entry-level jobs and the rapid adoption of AI.

To explore what this changing landscape means in practice, we brought together four people with different perspectives on the freelance economy. Mark Slack, a freelance creative director, and Sibusisiwe Khupe, a freelance creative and content creator, offer the view from the freelance side, while Mat Goff, co-founder of independent agency Ark, and Ben Major, global talent director at Uncommon Creative Studio, consider how agencies are adapting.

A MORE FLEXIBLE MODEL

Mat Goff: In a lot of people’s heads in the industry, you’re either an agency and therefore quite big, with lots of retained staff, or you’re really small and you bring people in as and when you need them. I think that is slightly old-school thinking and misses the point that you can be a good small agency with a retained core and then flex as and when you need across the various departments or creative disciplines. So we’re deliberately in that middle ground.

Ben Major: Lots of agencies are hedging their bets, and their ratio of freelance to permanent is sometimes 50-50. Sometimes that’s because you want specialist talent, and sometimes it’s in fear that you’re going to lose an account and you need to drop your biggest costs. So I think there are advantages to this agility we’re now seeing.

Flexibility needs to be met with flexibility. The expectation on companies is high, but I don’t know that that flexibility has washed through to everybody yet

MG: The flexibility piece is so important, because you might need a senior producer for five months to work on production, or you might want a junior creative team to look at some social work for five days. Having the ability to flex the amount of time you’re asking of those people is super important. And it cuts both ways. If you’re a small company and you’re pitching for a project, and you go out looking for a senior creative team, the day rate on those two people is gonna blow your project budget very quickly.

So, flexibility needs to meet with flexibility. I might go, ‘I only need you for three days, and I only really need one of you.’ The expectation on companies to be flexible is high, but I don’t know that that flexibility has washed through to everybody in the freelance market as yet.

Mark Slack: I never set out to be freelance. I was one of those CDs at a big agency, and a new CCO came in and cleared the floor of creative directors. All of a sudden I was thrown out into the world. Now when I go in as a CD, you can feel a little bit like a supply teacher.

Sibusisiwe Khupe: I was at Wieden+Kennedy up until last year. I sent a cold email, and the subject line was, ‘Free Gary Barlow tickets’, and they clicked on it. I got to make so much great work, but then they had a wide reshuffle and restructuring going on, so unfortunately I was let go. I just leapt into the world of freelance. I managed to get a freelance contract from September through March of this year. I’ve also been making content at the same time. I started in February and that has picked up quite a lot.

A NEW ROUTE INTO THE INDUSTRY

BM: Lots of people starting their career have no choice but to start freelance. And then it’s a very odd thing to engage a 21-year-old who’s never [worked in the industry]. What I tend to find is a lot of the people coming through just found their own way in. Call it a hustle mindset or overconfidence … it’s having that almost naïvety to contact an agency and be like, ‘I’m a creative, I can go do these things.’

SK: You need grit to be able to do things you wouldn’t normally think of doing. You need grit to be able to post your portfolio on Instagram. You need grit to be able to go on LinkedIn and say, ‘Hi guys, I do this, and I’m really good.’
In order to break through, you have to take the stage a little bit. You need to have audacity.

There was a guy when I was at Wieden’s who wanted to be part of the internship programme. He’d papered his shoe like a foot and left it in reception, and the copy was something like, ‘This is me trying to get my foot in the door.’

MS: It’s difficult for younger people because you’ve got to have a proven track record. Sometimes you just want freelancers to come in and fix something, rather than having a CD or a team where you’re thinking, ‘We’ve hired lots of younger people and it takes up a lot of our time.’ I think often it’s about going in and sussing a place out, understanding how it works. You’ve almost got to act like a mini agency yourself.

You’ve got to have conviction and present stuff as if it’s going straight to the client, rather than as if someone is going to take it and develop it.

THE MISSING MIDDLE

BM: There are so many long-term, journeyman freelancers that have spent their whole career working in a way that has really suited their life, and suddenly they’ve been out of work for six months. Before they know it, they’re in this really weird spot, where they haven’t really made anything because they’ve been drafted in for the rubbish-type briefs because the bigger shops will just get a freelancer to do the thing that no one wants to do. And so suddenly their portfolio looks a bit dull or old. It feels like they’re the group that’s been most affected in all of this.

You need grit to be able to do things that you wouldn’t normally think of doing. In order to break through, you have to take the stage a little bit. You need to have audacity

MS: I’m not feeling that positive about the situation now, to be totally honest. I think there are probably more of us senior, more expensive freelancers now, but it feels like there are fewer briefs around. Probably 80% of my time is trying to get the job and 20% is doing it. You’re faced with a day of scrabbling around for stuff for next week, that’s the worst bit.

But you just never know what’s around the corner. It’s still amazing how agencies literally go, ‘we need someone for three months’, on a Friday afternoon. I still find that baffling, but that’s just the way it is.

MG: It’s a challenge because senior people have bigger overheads and demand more money, and they may say, ‘Well, am I being excluded because of my age?’ Honestly, I don’t look at how old someone is. I don’t care. But if you want £800 a day and the next person wants £300 a day, then that’s a relatively straightforward decision for me to make.

My point is, some of the freelance market still operates like the industry is the same as it was 15 or 20 years ago. But the industry has changed, which means the economy of it has changed, and the companies within it have changed the way they behave and the way they work.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by sibusisiwe (@sibusisiiwe)

WHO GETS TO FREELANCE?

BM: The talent pool of freelancers isn’t as diverse as it should be. It’s still a huge problem for people of colour and class. Some are privileged enough to not have to worry about paying their rent for six weeks while they hustle for a semi-paid gig. Others aren’t, and that’s why the junior situation can’t just be totally reliant on them winging it, or the sort of token internships that still exist. Agencies have to commit to young talent, otherwise the whole thing falls apart.

My strategy around it has always been this: build the industry we wish existed. It’s not, build the Uncommon I wish existed – it’s the industry. We’re trying to improve creative education with Ravensbourne, we’re partnering with Yellowzine around their Mad Academy, we’re putting money into our own D&I. But it’s a tricky one, because those at the top are in a totally different economy to those at the bottom.

I’m not feeling that positive about the situation now. I think there are more of us senior freelancers now, but it feels like there are fewer briefs around

SK: When you’re freelancing, you’re really alone in the wilderness. You don’t have the warm blanket of the corporate HR department, and you know that certain things aren’t protected with freelancing. But it has taught me to be a lot more grounded and be able to advocate for myself. I know how to ask for what I want. I spoke about grit, but you also need resilience – you need to be willing to fall flat on your face a thousand times.

So you need to be comfortable with rejection, and you also need to be comfortable putting yourself out there. I’ve had to become really, really good at listening out for social insights. I know what’s good and what isn’t, what would be put at the back of the deck and what would get a thumbs up around the table. I think I’m better at being creative in advertising because of my content, and my content is making me better at my creative advertising job. Both of them are working hand in hand.

BUILDING SOMETHING BETTER

MG: People often go, ‘It’s a pitch, let’s get some freelancers’, and then largely ignore the work they do or their opinions. It’s like, well, if you’re gonna ask people to think about this problem and come and be part of your team, then you’ve got to open yourself up to their ideas. That’s the value exchange. The industry has to get less frictionful and make better sense economically.

The application of resource against a project or a piece of work, and doing that in the old-school way, is unsustainable. It makes us too expensive for clients; it makes us too slow. It’s a massive challenge for big organisations, and I think it’s relatively straightforward for small ones.

MS: Even if I got a permanent position now, I probably wouldn’t feel safe. There are fewer bigger briefs now because no one wants a three- to five-year platform. I helped launch Together We Thrive for HSBC when I was at Saatchi, but it didn’t last because you get people moving on, or something happens in the world, so it’s no longer about thriving, it’s about surviving.

I kind of live in fear of what’s to come because I’ve got a family. I’ve got contacts, but I still have to send the cold emails and do the desperate LinkedIn posting. But I have to lean on serendipity because it always sort of works out. I think advertising is going to try to find a different way of doing things – and probably freelancers will have to as well.

SK: This might sound a bit too utopian, but I would like to see more agencies working with freelancers to develop briefs. I know that might be a hot mess, but I do really think that if big agencies were working with freelance creatives as early as the briefing stage, the work would be in better shape. There are sometimes briefs that come through that disguise themselves as culture-first or social-first, but they’re actually not, and by the time I’ve realised, it’s too late because I’m already in the booking.

A lot of us sleep on the fact that, if you’ve come up in the digital age, especially through TikTok, you can sniff out things.

entry.title: Shopify turns ideas into reality in new brand campaign
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Shopify turns ideas into reality in new brand campaign Its first collaboration with Mother Los Angeles shows how AI assistant Sidekick helps budding entrepreneurs get their businesses off the ground By Adam Woodward 16/11/2026 3:06 am E-commerce platform Shop
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Shopify turns ideas into reality in new brand campaign

Its first collaboration with Mother Los Angeles shows how AI assistant Sidekick helps budding entrepreneurs get their businesses off the ground

By Adam Woodward 16/11/2026 3:06 am

E-commerce platform Shopify is encouraging would-be entrepreneurs to take the plunge with Just An Idea, a new brand campaign that explores how AI is lowering the barriers to starting a business.

Created in partnership with Mother Los Angeles – the agency’s first work for Shopify – the campaign centres on the premise that while launching a business has traditionally required money, people and specialist knowledge, many of those obstacles are becoming easier to overcome. What remains essential, argues Shopify, is having a solid idea in the first place.

A two-minute film follows four sets of first-time entrepreneurs as they attempt to turn everyday observations into viable businesses, with Shopify’s AI-powered business assistant, Sidekick, helping them navigate the process.

The stories range from Milo, a fashion enthusiast who turns an accidental water stain on a sketch into the starting point for a clothing brand, to Walter, an office worker who develops a decorative window decal to stop birds flying into glass.

Elsewhere, a couple design a colourful sofa for dogs after struggling to find an appealing bed for their ageing pet, while a group of high school students develop personalised pimple patches.

Across each story, Sidekick helps with everything from developing brand identities and building online stores to finding manufacturers, writing product descriptions and planning launches. The entrepreneurs remain the focus though, with the technology positioned more as a means of getting their ideas off the ground.

The high-energy spot was directed by Marcus Ibanez through Iconoclast and shot on film by Kasper Tuxen, and is soundtracked to Forever Young by Swedish rapper Yung Lean.

“When Marcus brought us the pace of the film, it set the direction for everything else. It’s just on the verge of overwhelming, which helps us not only show what it’s like for entrepreneurs to try to realise their idea, but also pack a lot of story into a short amount of time,” said Tobias Lindborg, creative director at Mother.

entry.title: Apple’s Christmas ad celebrates the creative dreamers
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Apple’s Christmas ad celebrates the creative dreamers Directed by Melina Matsoukas and featuring artworks by Hebru Brantley, the four-minute film follows a child who loves to draw as he grows up By Eliza Williams 13/11/2026 3:52 am Apple’s Christmas ad for 20
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Apple’s Christmas ad celebrates the creative dreamers

Directed by Melina Matsoukas and featuring artworks by Hebru Brantley, the four-minute film follows a child who loves to draw as he grows up

By Eliza Williams 13/11/2026 3:52 am

Apple’s Christmas ad for 2026 is a thoughtful and poignant affair, focusing on the joys and struggles that a love of creativity can bring.

The film opens on a young child who has an innate passion and talent for drawing, so much so that his art soon spreads beyond the pages of his sketchbooks onto the walls of his house, much to his mother’s chagrin. We then watch him grow, going through teenage angst and into uncreative jobs, with his love of art still remaining a constant companion.

By the end of the film though, his art is more of a private, side endeavour, yet one that his parents wish to encourage – which they do by giving him the gift of an Macbook Neo laptop for Christmas, which then opens up new worlds of creative possibilities.

Writing it down, this storyline sounds kind of cheesy, though Matsoukas’ direction keeps it authentic and avoids the film falling into schmaltz. A delicate soundtrack of Give Me A Dream by Strawberry Guy treads a similar line.

The spot draws on several trends of this year. It is focused on craft, with all the artworks featured in the film created by Hebru Brantley, who shared his making-of story on his Instagram alongside the launch of the ad.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Hello Apple (@helloapple)

The appearance of Apple’s tech in the ad is subtle, though a scene of the father photographing his young son while he draws sees an old iPhone used, plugging into our current love for ‘vintage’ tech – and while this trend is arguably more for analogue tech, the sight of an old version of the iPhone is surprisingly charming.

Finally, the spot is firmly rooted in human creativity – there is no AI in sight, and where the tech plays a part it is as a tool that helps aid the creative act, bringing artistic dreams to life. At a time when we are all obsessing about big tech crushing creative opportunities, Apple is clearly hoping to remind audiences that it is there to support, not destroy.

Creative Process

Adam Sillard on finding pleasure in the creative process

The French illustrator and animator talks about the influences behind his images, the relationship between personal and commercial work, and why the best drawings don’t always go to plan

By Rebecca Fulleylove 13/11/2026 3:04 am

“I have learned to draw first and think later,” says illustrator and animator Adam Sillard. “Some of my best drawings are the ones that I made without knowing what I was doing and without thinking about the result too much.”

Sillard has drawn for as long as he can remember, but formalised his passion at Gobelins, the Paris school specialising in animation and visual arts. While he developed his skills in animation and art direction, the biggest benefit of being at the school came from the community he found.

“I mostly learned from meeting other young artists like myself, many of who have remained my friends today.”

entry.content:
Creative Insight

The rise of the employee creator

Employee-generated content is evolving beyond brand advocacy. CR explores the value of staff developing their own followings and identities, and the challenges this presents for brands

By Rebecca Fulleylove 12/11/2026 3:52 am

From M&S’s director of product development Kathryn Turner to Kaeden Rowland, the deadpan print specialist better known as the Staples Baddie, employees are becoming some of the most interesting new brand storytellers.
Waitrose, Hobbycraft and Waterstones’ local store accounts are also racking up views, while Starbucks and Gap have announced developments to their employee creator initiatives. It seems brands are happily looking inwards for a new generation of creative talent.

Employee-generated content (EGC) isn’t new, but what’s evolved is the ambition and creativity behind it. Rather than simply asking staff to share corporate messaging, brands are beginning to recognise employees as creators with the potential to build audiences around their own expertise and personalities.

But as staff build audiences and identities beyond their day jobs, brands face a new challenge. How much freedom are they prepared to give the people who represent them?

entry.title: Garip Studio creates playful identity for children’s arts school
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Garip Studio creates playful identity for children’s arts school The hand-drawn branding for Istanbul-based Güneş Ülkesi has been designed to reflect both its name and evolving cultural role By Adam Woodward 12/11/2026 3:26 am Turkish creative studio Garip St
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Garip Studio creates playful identity for children’s arts school

The hand-drawn branding for Istanbul-based Güneş Ülkesi has been designed to reflect both its name and evolving cultural role

By Adam Woodward 12/11/2026 3:26 am

Turkish creative studio Garip Studio has developed a colourful, hand-drawn identity for Güneş Ülkesi, a school that encourages children to explore the arts through movement, experimentation and play.

Founded in 2019, Güneş Ülkesi teaches ballet, music, painting and creative drama, primarily to children under the age of ten. Its approach encourages pupils to move freely between disciplines, building confidence while developing their own ways of seeing and making. As the school looks to expand its reach and bring more children into the arts, it wanted an identity that could reflect its ambitions and evolving cultural role.

The resulting visual identity takes its starting point from the school’s name, which translates as ‘Land of the Sun’. At its centre is a custom logotype, drawn entirely by hand and arranged in a circular composition to resemble a sun.

Rather than functioning simply as a wordmark, the lettering becomes the identity’s primary visual device, informing everything from printed materials to digital communications and the school’s physical spaces.

The colour palette follows the same solar inspiration, combining bright yellow, warm orange and soft beige, with black marks introduced according to context. Halyard Display by Darden Studio provides a more restrained typographic counterpoint to the expressive lettering.

The identity also incorporates a series of animated elements, with individual motion pieces developed for each of the school’s disciplines. Lesson animations, inspired by the typography, are used to announce classes, while the lettering’s variable, free-flowing character allows the wider system to be continually reinterpreted across the school’s activities and performances.

For Bertuğ Bilgin, founder and creative director of Garip Studio, the aim was to capture something of the uninhibited imagination that defines childhood. “The sun is one of the first things almost every child draws. We built the identity around that, and around the uninhibited imagination of the children themselves,” he says.

He adds: “We wanted the lettering to do more than sign off the brand. It gives the whole identity its movement, rhythm and sense of play, so it feels as free as the children who learn there.”
